claim: Fast rhythmic activity in the prefrontal cortex becomes prominent during the second postnatal week.
source: We show that fast rhythmic activity in the prefrontal cortex becomes prominent during the second postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data from extracellular recordings shown in Figure 1.

claim: Fast oscillatory activity initially occurs at about 15 Hz.
source: While initially at about 15 Hz, fast oscillatory activity progressively accelerates with age and stabilizes within gamma frequency range (30–80 Hz) during the fourth postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1 showing peak frequencies starting at ~20 Hz at P12.

claim: Fast oscillatory activity stabilizes within gamma frequency range (30–80 Hz) during the fourth postnatal week.
source: While initially at about 15 Hz, fast oscillatory activity progressively accelerates with age and stabilizes within gamma frequency range (30–80 Hz) during the fourth postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing stabilization at 50-60 Hz at P25 in Figure 1.

claim: Activation of layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons drives fast oscillations throughout development.
source: Activation of layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons drives fast oscillations throughout development, yet the acceleration of their frequency follows similar temporal dynamics as the maturation of fast-spiking interneurons.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by optogenetic stimulation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The acceleration of fast oscillation frequency follows similar temporal dynamics as the maturation of fast-spiking interneurons.
source: Activation of layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons drives fast oscillations throughout development, yet the acceleration of their frequency follows similar temporal dynamics as the maturation of fast-spiking interneurons.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data comparing FS interneuron maturation (Figure 2) with gamma frequency development (Figure 1).

claim: Gamma oscillations are a prominent activity pattern in the cerebral cortex.
source: Gamma oscillations are a prominent activity pattern in the cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge presented in the abstract.

claim: Oscillatory activity in gamma frequency range has been proposed to organize neuronal ensembles and to shape information processing in cortical networks.
source: While its exact functions are still a matter of debate, oscillatory activity in gamma frequency range has been proposed to organize neuronal ensembles and to shape information processing in cortical networks (Singer, 2018; Cardin, 2016; Sohal, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Gamma activity emerges from reciprocal interactions between excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Gamma activity emerges from reciprocal interactions between excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field, presented in the introduction.

claim: In the visual cortex, fast inhibitory feedback via soma-targeting parvalbumin (PV)-expressing inhibitory interneurons leads to fast gamma activity (30–80 Hz).
source: In the visual cortex, fast inhibitory feedback via soma-targeting parvalbumin (PV)-expressing inhibitory interneurons leads to fast gamma activity (30–80 Hz) (Cardin et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dendrite-targeting somatostatin (SOM)-expressing inhibitory interneurons contribute to beta/low gamma activity (20–40 Hz).
source: whereas dendrite-targeting somatostatin (SOM)-expressing inhibitory interneurons contribute to beta/low gamma activity (20–40 Hz) (Chen et al., 2017; Veit et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Interneuronal dysfunction and ensuing abnormal gamma activity in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) have been linked to impaired cognitive flexibility.
source: Interneuronal dysfunction and ensuing abnormal gamma activity in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) have been linked to impaired cognitive flexibility (Cho et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Imbalance between excitation and inhibition in cortical networks and resulting gamma disruption have been proposed to cause cognitive disabilities in autism and schizophrenia.
source: Moreover, imbalance between excitation and inhibition in cortical networks and resulting gamma disruption have been proposed to cause cognitive disabilities in autism and schizophrenia (Cho et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2018; Rojas and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The ontogeny of prefrontal gamma activity is poorly understood.
source: Despite substantial literature linking cognitive abilities and disabilities to gamma oscillations in the adult mPFC, the ontogeny of prefrontal gamma activity is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Abnormal patterns of fast oscillatory activity have been described at early postnatal age in autism and schizophrenia mouse models.
source: This knowledge gap is even more striking considering that abnormal patterns of fast oscillatory activity have been described at early postnatal age in autism and schizophrenia mouse models (Chini et al., 2020; Richter et al., 2019; Hartung et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Oscillatory activity at fast frequencies (>12 Hz) can be detected in the mPFC at the beginning of the second postnatal week.
source: Extracellular recordings in the mPFC of anesthetized and non-anesthetized P5-40 mice revealed that oscillatory activity at fast frequencies (>12 Hz) can be detected at the beginning of the second postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from extracellular recordings.

claim: The temporal dynamics of fast oscillations are similar in anesthetized and non-anesthetized states, yet their magnitude is higher in non-anesthetized mice.
source: The temporal dynamics of these fast oscillations are similar in the two states, yet their magnitude is higher in non-anesthetized mice, as previously described (Chini et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The magnitude of fast oscillations increases with age.
source: The magnitude of fast oscillations increases with age (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=3.93×10−22, n = 114 recordings, tau-b 0.625)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Fast oscillations can be detected as distinct peaks in power spectra at the end of the second postnatal week.
source: The magnitude of fast oscillations increases with age (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=3.93×10−22, n = 114 recordings, tau-b 0.625) and can be detected as distinct peaks in power spectra at the end of the second postnatal week (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The peak frequency of fast oscillations gradually increases with age.
source: The peak frequency of these oscillations gradually increases with age (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=2.73×10−8, n = 114 recordings, tau-b 0.361)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Fast oscillations start at ~ 20 Hz at P12.
source: The peak frequency of these oscillations gradually increases with age (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=2.73×10−8, n = 114 recordings, tau-b 0.361), starting at ~ 20 Hz at P12 and reaching the characteristic gamma frequency of 50–60 Hz at P25 (Figure 1b–d).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Fast oscillations reach the characteristic gamma frequency of 50–60 Hz at P25.
source: The peak frequency of these oscillations gradually increases with age (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=2.73×10−8, n = 114 recordings, tau-b 0.361), starting at ~ 20 Hz at P12 and reaching the characteristic gamma frequency of 50–60 Hz at P25 (Figure 1b–d).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Peak strength and peak frequency do not change after P25.
source: Both, peak strength and peak frequency, do not change after P25.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: Peak frequency and peak amplitude show significant correlation with age.
source: A linear regression model of peak frequency and peak amplitude shows significant correlation with age (n = 114, df = 111, R2 = 0.542, p=5.48×10−20; ANOVA: peak frequency F(1,111)=17.8, p=4.86×10−5, peak amplitude F(1,111)=74.4, p=5.05×10−14).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: PV expression in the mPFC starts at the end of the second postnatal week.
source: First, immunostainings showed that PV expression in the mPFC starts at the end of the second postnatal week, increases until P25 and stabilizes afterwards (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=1.29×10−7, n = 38 mice, tau-b 0.623) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: PV expression increases until P25 and stabilizes afterwards.
source: First, immunostainings showed that PV expression in the mPFC starts at the end of the second postnatal week, increases until P25 and stabilizes afterwards (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=1.29×10−7, n = 38 mice, tau-b 0.623) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The developmental dynamics of PV expression follow a similar trend as the changes in peak power and peak frequency of fast oscillations.
source: These dynamics over age follow a similar trend as the changes in peak power and peak frequency of the fast oscillations described above.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of PV expression data with oscillation data.

claim: The number of SOM positive neurons does not significantly vary along postnatal development.
source: In contrast, the number of SOM positive neurons does not significantly vary along postnatal development (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=0.99, n = 39 mice, tau-b −0.003) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: FS units start to be detected at the end of the second postnatal week.
source: The classification of units with this method revealed that FS units start to be detected at the end of the second postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is based on single unit analysis using t-sne dimensionality reduction and hierarchical clustering.

claim: The number of FS units gradually increased until P25.
source: Their number gradually increased until P25 (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=1.44×10−7, n = 66 recordings, tau-b 0.458) (Figure 2h).
evidence: This claim is based on single unit analysis data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Trough-to-peak duration of RS and FS units gradually decreased from the end of the second postnatal week until P25.
source: A comparison of the classical features across age showed that trough-to-peak duration (Mann-Kendall trend test, RS, p=4.57×10−5, n = 3172 units, tau-b −0.051; FS, p=9.23×10−11, n = 382 units, tau-b −0.236), half width (Mann-Kendall trend test, RS, p=1.61×10−28, n = 3172 units, tau-b −0.134; FS, p=5.17×10−17, n = 382 units, tau-b −0.295), and negative amplitude (Mann-Kendall trend test, RS, p=4.45×10−22, n = 3172 units, tau-b −0.117; FS, p=3.82×10−6, n = 382 units, tau-b −0.163) of RS and FS units gradually decreased from the end of the second postnatal week until P25.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of single unit waveform features.

claim: Half width of RS and FS units gradually decreased from the end of the second postnatal week until P25.
source: A comparison of the classical features across age showed that trough-to-peak duration (Mann-Kendall trend test, RS, p=4.57×10−5, n = 3172 units, tau-b −0.051; FS, p=9.23×10−11, n = 382 units, tau-b −0.236), half width (Mann-Kendall trend test, RS, p=1.61×10−28, n = 3172 units, tau-b −0.134; FS, p=5.17×10−17, n = 382 units, tau-b −0.295), and negative amplitude (Mann-Kendall trend test, RS, p=4.45×10−22, n = 3172 units, tau-b −0.117; FS, p=3.82×10−6, n = 382 units, tau-b −0.163) of RS and FS units gradually decreased from the end of the second postnatal week until P25.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of single unit waveform features.

claim: Negative amplitude of RS and FS units gradually decreased from the end of the second postnatal week until P25.
source: A comparison of the classical features across age showed that trough-to-peak duration (Mann-Kendall trend test, RS, p=4.57×10−5, n = 3172 units, tau-b −0.051; FS, p=9.23×10−11, n = 382 units, tau-b −0.236), half width (Mann-Kendall trend test, RS, p=1.61×10−28, n = 3172 units, tau-b −0.134; FS, p=5.17×10−17, n = 382 units, tau-b −0.295), and negative amplitude (Mann-Kendall trend test, RS, p=4.45×10−22, n = 3172 units, tau-b −0.117; FS, p=3.82×10−6, n = 382 units, tau-b −0.163) of RS and FS units gradually decreased from the end of the second postnatal week until P25.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of single unit waveform features.

claim: The most prominent changes in waveform features were detected for through-to-peak duration and half width of FS units.
source: However, the most prominent changes were detected for through-to-peak duration and half width of FS units (Figure 2i).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of single unit waveform data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Single unit features show significant correlation with age.
source: A linear regression model of single unit features shows significant correlation with age (n = 52, df = 44, R2 = 0.550, p=2.31×10−7; see Supplementary file 2 for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of single unit data.

claim: The time course of the maturation of FS units is consistent with a detailed description of the physiological development of prefrontal PV-expressing interneurons performed in brain slices.
source: These results are consistent with a detailed description of the physiological development of prefrontal PV-expressing interneurons performed in brain slices (Miyamae et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with previous literature.

claim: The functional maturation of FS PV-expressing interneurons shows similar dynamics of maturation as fast oscillations recorded in the mPFC of P5-40 mice.
source: Thus, in line with the immunohistochemical examination, the analysis of single units showed that FS putatively PV-positive interneurons show similar dynamics of maturation as fast oscillations recorded in the mPFC of P5-40 mice.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of FS interneuron maturation data with oscillation data.

claim: L2/3 PYRs in mPFC induce fast oscillations in the mPFC of P8-10 mice.
source: Besides FS interneurons, L2/3 PYRs in mPFC have been found to induce fast oscillations in the mPFC of P8-10 mice.
evidence: This claim references previous findings.

claim: Non-rhythmic activation of L2/3 PYRs (but not activation of L5/6PYRs) drives oscillatory activity peaking within 15–20 Hz range.
source: Their non-rhythmic activation (but not activation of L5/6PYRs) drives oscillatory activity peaking within 15–20 Hz range (Bitzenhofer et al., 2017a; Bitzenhofer et al., 2017b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stable expression of ChR2(ET/TC) restricted to about 25% of PYR in L2/3 of the mPFC was achieved by in utero electroporation at E15.5.
source: Stable expression of the light-sensitive channelrhodopsin two derivate E123T T159C (ChR2(ET/TC)) restricted to about 25% of PYR in L2/3 of the mPFC was achieved by in utero electroporation (IUE) at embryonic day (E) 15.5 (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method and is supported by Figure 3a.

claim: Activating L2/3 PYRs induced oscillatory activity with a gradually increasing frequency during development.
source: Similar to spontaneous activity, activating L2/3 PYRs induced oscillatory activity with a gradually increasing frequency during development (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This claim is based on optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Consistent peaks in the modulation index of power spectra were detected at 15–20 Hz at the beginning of the second postnatal week.
source: Consistent peaks in the modulation index (MI) of power spectra were detected at 15–20 Hz at the beginning of the second postnatal week and increased in frequency (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=7.69×10−6, n = 115 recordings, tau-b 0.288) and amplitude (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=1.04×10−9, n = 115 recordings, tau-b 0.392) until reaching stable values within 50–60 Hz at P25.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of optogenetic stimulation data.

claim: L2/3 PYR-induced oscillations increased in frequency and amplitude until reaching stable values within 50–60 Hz at P25.
source: Consistent peaks in the modulation index (MI) of power spectra were detected at 15–20 Hz at the beginning of the second postnatal week and increased in frequency (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=7.69×10−6, n = 115 recordings, tau-b 0.288) and amplitude (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=1.04×10−9, n = 115 recordings, tau-b 0.392) until reaching stable values within 50–60 Hz at P25.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of optogenetic stimulation data.

claim: Control stimulations with light that does not activate ChR2(ET/TC) did not induce activity and led to the detection of unspecific peak frequencies.
source: Control stimulations with light that does not activate ChR2(ET/TC) (594 nm, 3 s, 30 repetitions) did not induce activity and led to the detection of unspecific peak frequencies (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=0.09, n = 111 recordings, tau-b 0.111) and low amplitudes (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=0.74, n = 111 recordings, tau-b 0.022) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Peak frequency and amplitude of activity induced by ramp light stimulation are significantly correlated with peak frequency and amplitude of spontaneous activity at the level of individual recordings.
source: Peak frequency and amplitude of activity induced by ramp light stimulation are significantly correlated with peak frequency and amplitude of spontaneous activity at the level of individual recordings (peak frequency n = 114, df = 112, R2 = 0.16, p=6.00×10−6; peak amplitude n = 114, df = 112, R2 = 0.206, p=2.30×10−7).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing spontaneous and induced activity.

claim: L2/3 PYR-driven activity in the mPFC follows the same developmental dynamics as spontaneous activity.
source: Thus, L2/3 PYR-driven activity in the mPFC follows the same developmental dynamics as spontaneous activity indicating the importance of L2/3 PYRs for gamma maturation.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of optogenetically-induced and spontaneous activity data.

claim: The average firing rate of RS and FS units in the stimulated hemisphere in the mPFC increased in response to ramp stimulation.
source: The average firing rate of RS and FS units in the stimulated hemisphere in the mPFC increased in response to ramp stimulation (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is based on single unit analysis during optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Ramp-induced firing rate changes averaged for RS units became more prominent at older age.
source: While ramp-induced firing rate changes averaged for RS units (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=0.07, n = 7 age groups, tau-b 0.619) became more prominent at older age, the average firing rate changes were stable for FS units (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=0.88, n = 7 age groups, tau-b 0.047) (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of single unit firing rates shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The average firing rate changes were stable for FS units across development.
source: While ramp-induced firing rate changes averaged for RS units (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=0.07, n = 7 age groups, tau-b 0.619) became more prominent at older age, the average firing rate changes were stable for FS units (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=0.88, n = 7 age groups, tau-b 0.047) (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of single unit firing rates shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Most RS units showed positive modulation of their firing rates in response to stimulation at P5-10.
source: At the level of individual units, most RS units showed positive modulation of their firing rates in response to stimulation at P5-10, whereas at older age the proportion of positively modulated units decreased (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=1.52×10−14, n = 1821 units, tau-b −0.123) (Figure 4e).
evidence: This claim is based on single unit analysis shown in Figure 4e.

claim: At older age the proportion of positively modulated RS units decreased.
source: At the level of individual units, most RS units showed positive modulation of their firing rates in response to stimulation at P5-10, whereas at older age the proportion of positively modulated units decreased (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=1.52×10−14, n = 1821 units, tau-b −0.123) (Figure 4e).
evidence: This claim is based on single unit analysis shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Individual FS units showed both positive and negative modulation of activity throughout development.
source: In contrast, individual FS units showed both positive and negative modulation of activity throughout development (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=0.91, n = 225 units, tau-b −0.005)
evidence: This claim is based on single unit analysis of FS units.

claim: A subset of RS and FS units fire rhythmically in response to ramp light stimulation of prefrontal L2/3 PYRs.
source: While no clear peaks of rhythmicity were found during spontaneous activity before stimulations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), autocorrelations showed that a subset of RS and FS units fire rhythmically in response to ramp light stimulation of prefrontal L2/3 PYRs (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is based on autocorrelation analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Prominent rhythmic firing starts at about P15 and increases in frequency before it stabilizes at about P25.
source: The power of autocorrelations revealed that prominent rhythmic firing starts at about P15 and increases in frequency before it stabilizes at about P25 (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is based on autocorrelation power analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The development of spike-triggered LFP power is consistent with the development of single unit autocorrelation power.
source: Next, we calculated the power of averaged spike-triggered LFPs to examine the interaction of single unit rhythmicity with oscillatory LFP activity. The development of spike-triggered LFP power is consistent with the development of single unit autocorrelation power (multifactorial ANOVA: unit type F(1,814825) = 277.2, p=3.12×10−62, age group F(6,814825) = 847.4, p=0.000, frequency F(400, 814825)=614.5, p=0.000)
evidence: This claim is based on spike-triggered LFP analysis.

claim: Single unit rhythmicity of local neurons is reflected in the prefrontal LFP.
source: The development of spike-triggered LFP power is consistent with the development of single unit autocorrelation power (multifactorial ANOVA: unit type F(1,814825) = 277.2, p=3.12×10−62, age group F(6,814825) = 847.4, p=0.000, frequency F(400, 814825)=614.5, p=0.000), indicating that single unit rhythmicity of local neurons is reflected in the prefrontal LFP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the consistency between single unit and LFP data.

claim: RS units show higher values at lower instantaneous frequencies for inter-spike intervals than FS units.
source: RS units show higher values at lower instantaneous frequencies for inter-spike intervals than FS units, suggesting that they tend to skip cycles of induced gamma activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This claim is based on inter-spike interval analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2d.

claim: RS units tend to skip cycles of induced gamma activity.
source: RS units show higher values at lower instantaneous frequencies for inter-spike intervals than FS units, suggesting that they tend to skip cycles of induced gamma activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This claim is inferred from inter-spike interval data.

claim: The dynamics of RS and FS rhythmicity are similar to the development of spontaneous and stimulated gamma activity.
source: Overall, the dynamics of RS and FS rhythmicity are similar to the development of spontaneous and stimulated gamma activity, indicating close interactions between RS and FS units during fast oscillations.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of single unit rhythmicity with LFP oscillation data.

claim: RS units did not follow high stimulation frequencies in mice younger than P11 and showed strong attenuation in the response to repetitive pulses.
source: Confirming previous results (Bitzenhofer et al., 2017a), RS units did not follow high stimulation frequencies in mice younger than P11 and showed strong attenuation in the response to repetitive pulses.
evidence: This claim is based on pulse stimulation experiments and confirmed by citation to previous work.

claim: With ongoing development, attenuation at high stimulation frequencies became less prominent for RS and FS units.
source: With ongoing development, this attenuation at high stimulation frequencies became less prominent for RS and FS units (Figure 6b)
evidence: This claim is based on pulse stimulation data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Individual units do not fire in response to every light pulse in the pulse train but skip some pulses.
source: Inter-spike intervals of individual units revealed several peaks at fractions of the stimulation frequency for RS and FS, especially at higher stimulation frequencies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). These data suggest that individual units do not fire in response to every light pulse in the pulse train but skip some pulses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from inter-spike interval data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The firing rate of RS and FS units transiently increased after pulse stimulation.
source: The firing rate of RS and FS units transiently increased after pulse stimulation (Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is based on pulse stimulation data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The transient increase in firing rate significantly increased with age for RS units.
source: This effect significantly increased with age for RS units (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=0.04, n = 7 age groups, tau-b 0.714), but not for FS units (Mann-Kendall trend test, p=0.07, n = 7 age groups, tau-b 0.619) (Figure 6d).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of firing rate changes shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The similar delays observed for RS and FS units suggest that the majority of RS units are non-transfected neurons, that are indirectly activated.
source: Next, we analyzed the delays of light-induced firing peaks for the two populations of units. The similar delays observed for RS and FS units suggest that the majority of RS units are non-transfected neurons, that are indirectly activated.
evidence: This claim is inferred from analysis of firing peak delays.

claim: The initial peak of increased firing was followed by reduced firing rates for RS and FS units only during late postnatal development.
source: The initial peak of increased firing was followed by reduced firing rates for RS and FS units only during late postnatal development (Figure 6e,f).
evidence: This claim is based on firing rate analysis shown in Figure 6e,f.

claim: The magnitude and duration of firing depression gradually augmented with age and reached significance for RS units.
source: The magnitude and duration of this firing depression gradually augmented with age and reached significance for RS units (Mann-Kendall trend test, RS, p=6.9×10−3, n = 7 age groups, tau-b −0.905; FS, p=0.07, n = 7 age groups, tau-b −0.619).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of firing depression data.

claim: The inhibitory feedback in response to L2/3 PYR firing in the mPFC increases with age.
source: Thus, the inhibitory feedback in response to L2/3 PYR firing in the mPFC increases with age.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the firing depression data.

claim: Action potential half width of FS units and peak power of autocorrelation of RS and FS units are the best predictor variables for peak frequency during ramp light stimulation.
source: Stepwise linear regression to predict the peak frequency during ramp light stimulation identified action potential half width of FS units, as well as peak power of autocorrelation of RS and FS units as best predictor variables (n = 42, df = 38, R2 = 0.136, p=0.036; see Supplementary file 2 for detailed statistics).
evidence: This claim is based on stepwise linear regression analysis.

claim: Firing rate change of RS units during ramp light stimulation, peak power of spike-triggered LFP for RS units, RS firing rate change 0–10 ms after pulse stimulation, and FS firing rate change 10–50 ms after pulse stimulation are the best predictor variables for peak amplitude during ramp light stimulation.
source: Stepwise linear regression to predict the peak amplitude during ramp light stimulation identified firing rate change of RS units during ramp light stimulation, peak power of spike-triggered LFP for RS units, as well as RS firing rate change 0–10 ms after pulse stimulation and FS firing rate change 10–50 ms after pulse stimulation as best predictor variables (n = 48, df = 43, R2 = 0.716, p=4.35×10−12; see Supplementary file 2 for detailed statistics).
evidence: This claim is based on stepwise linear regression analysis.

claim: Peak amplitude during ramp light stimulation is correlated with firing rate changes in response to ramp and pulse stimulations.
source: Thus, peak amplitude during ramp light stimulation is correlated with firing rate changes in response to ramp and pulse stimulations, indicating the importance of stimulation efficacy for peak amplitude.
evidence: This claim is based on regression analysis results.

claim: FS characteristics and rhythmicity of single units show the strongest correlation with the peak frequency of LFP power.
source: On the other hand, FS characteristics and rhythmicity of single units show the strongest correlation with the peak frequency of LFP power.
evidence: This claim is based on regression analysis results.

claim: Fast synaptic inhibition of the perisomatic region of pyramidal neurons by PV-expressing interneurons is critical for the generation of gamma oscillations.
source: Specifically, fast synaptic inhibition of the perisomatic region of pyramidal neurons by PV-expressing interneurons is critical for the generation of gamma oscillations (Cardin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Suppressing PV-expressing interneurons in the adult mPFC reduces the power in gamma frequency and impairs interhemispheric synchronization and cognitive abilities.
source: Suppressing PV-expressing interneurons in the adult mPFC reduces the power in gamma frequency and impairs interhemispheric synchronization and cognitive abilities (Cho et al., 2015; Cho et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The functional maturation of FS PV-expressing interneurons and single unit rhythmicity of RS and FS units are best correlated with the accelerating gamma activity in the LFP.
source: Further, we show that the functional maturation of FS PV-expressing interneurons and single unit rhythmicity of RS and FS units are best correlated with the accelerating gamma activity in the LFP.
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from the regression analysis.

claim: The acceleration toward higher frequencies relates to the maturation of inhibitory feedback and of FS interneurons.
source: While activation of L2/3 PYR drives fast oscillatory activity throughout development, the acceleration toward higher frequencies relates to the maturation of inhibitory feedback and of FS interneurons.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The interplay between excitatory and inhibitory neurons is critical for the generation of adult gamma activity and for its emergence during postnatal development.
source: These results suggest that the interplay between excitatory and inhibitory neurons is not only critical for the generation of adult gamma activity but also for its emergence during postnatal development.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The L2/3 PYRs-driven oscillatory activity was strongly correlated with spontaneously occurring fast frequency oscillations.
source: The L2/3 PYRs-driven oscillatory activity was strongly correlated with spontaneously occurring fast frequency oscillations.
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis between spontaneous and induced activity.

claim: Broader peaks in power spectra for spontaneous activity indicate that the stimulation-induced activity might not cover the full diversity of spontaneous gamma activity.
source: However, broader peaks in power spectra for spontaneous activity indicate that the stimulation-induced activity might not cover the full diversity of spontaneous gamma activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of spontaneous and induced activity spectra.

claim: The broadness of spontaneous activity gamma power might explain the absence of clear locking and rhythmicity of single units in the absence of prefrontal stimulation or task-induced activation of the mPFC.
source: The broadness of spontaneous activity gamma power might also explain the absence of clear locking and rhythmicity of single units in the absence of prefrontal stimulation or task-induced activation of the mPFC.
evidence: This claim is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Classical frequency bands (i.e. delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma) are largely preserved between different mammalian species.
source: These 'classical' frequency bands (i.e. delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma) are largely preserved between different mammalian species (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004; Buzsáki et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Synchronization of cortical areas in fast oscillatory rhythms starts during the first postnatal week.
source: Synchronization of cortical areas in fast oscillatory rhythms starts during the first postnatal week (Brockmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Low-amplitude patterns are detected in the rodent mPFC as early as P5, 1–2 days later compared to primary sensory cortices (S1, V1).
source: These low-amplitude patterns are detected in the rodent mPFC as early as P5,1–2 days later compared to primary sensory cortices (S1, V1) (Minlebaev et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013; Dupont et al., 2006; Shen and Colonnese, 2016; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neonatal fast activity has a relative low frequency (around 20 Hz).
source: However, this neonatal fast activity has a relative low frequency (around 20 Hz) (Brockmann et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the developing mPFC the detection of prominent fast oscillations with frequencies above 12 Hz coincides with the switch from discontinuous to continuous activity.
source: We previously showed that in the developing mPFC the detection of prominent fast oscillations with frequencies above 12 Hz coincides with the switch from discontinuous to continuous activity (Brockmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim references previous findings by the authors.

claim: A similar increase in gamma frequency has been previously described after eye opening in the visual cortex.
source: A similar increase in gamma frequency has been previously described after eye opening in the visual cortex (Hoy and Niell, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Identification of oscillatory patterns in developing circuits according to 'classical' frequency bands established for adults should be avoided.
source: Therefore, identification of oscillatory patterns in developing circuits according to 'classical' frequency bands established for adults should be avoided.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: PV expression and FS characteristics do not completely overlap.
source: Since PV expression and FS characteristics do not completely overlap (Ma et al., 2006; Onorato et al., 2020), the method has the same drawback as that typically used for the distinction of adult RS and FS and cannot identify RS interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FS units are detected in the mPFC during the second postnatal week and progressively mature until the fourth postnatal week, consistent with PV interneuron maturation.
source: We demonstrate that FS units are detected in the mPFC during the second postnatal week and progressively mature until the fourth postnatal week, consistent with PV interneuron maturation (Okaty et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the absence of FS interneurons at early age, inhibitory feedback from SOM neurons might contribute to early oscillatory activity at frequencies within 12–20 Hz range.
source: In the absence of FS interneurons at early age, inhibitory feedback from SOM neurons – important for slow gamma activity in the adult cortex (Veit et al., 2017) – might contribute to early oscillatory activity at frequencies within 12–20 Hz range.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the data and supported by a citation.

claim: An in-depth investigation of prefrontal PYRs during development had identified prominent changes in their dendritic arborization, passive and active membrane properties, as well as excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
source: While we only found minor age-dependent changes in the extracellular waveforms of RS units, an in-depth investigation of prefrontal PYRs during development had identified prominent changes in their dendritic arborization, passive and active membrane properties, as well as excitatory and inhibitory inputs (Kroon et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Changes in pyramidal neuron properties most likely contribute to the maturation of pyramidal-interneuronal interactions and finally, of gamma activity.
source: These changes, even though not detected with extracellular recordings, most likely contribute to the maturation of pyramidal-interneuronal interactions and finally, of gamma activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous literature and the current findings.

claim: The maturation of inhibitory feedback in response to prefrontal L2/3 PYRs stimulation follows the same dynamics as the development of gamma oscillations.
source: Indeed, we found that the maturation of inhibitory feedback in response to prefrontal L2/3 PYRs stimulation follows the same dynamics as the development of gamma oscillations.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data comparing inhibitory feedback with gamma development.

claim: Rhythmicity of single RS and FS units were identified as good predictors for the frequencies of oscillatory activity.
source: Furthermore, rhythmicity of single RS and FS units were identified as good predictors for the frequencies of oscillatory activity.
evidence: This claim is based on regression analysis results.

claim: GABAergic transmission in the rodent cortex matures during postnatal development, reaching an adult-like state toward the end of the fourth postnatal week.
source: GABAergic transmission in the rodent cortex matures during postnatal development, reaching an adult-like state toward the end of the fourth postnatal week (Le Magueresse and Monyer, 2013; Butt et al., 2017; Lim et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Shortly after birth, GABA acts depolarizing due to high intracellular chloride in immature neurons expressing low levels of the chloride cotransporter KCC2 relative to NKCC1.
source: Shortly after birth, GABA acts depolarizing due to high intracellular chloride in immature neurons expressing low levels of the chloride cotransporter KCC2 relative to NKCC1 (Rivera et al., 1999; Lim et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depolarization by GABA is not sufficient to trigger action potential firing and results in shunting inhibition.
source: However, this depolarization is not sufficient to trigger action potential firing and results in shunting inhibition (Kirmse et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The switch of GABA action from depolarizing to hyperpolarizing has been reported to occur during the second postnatal week.
source: The switch of GABA action from depolarizing to hyperpolarizing has been reported to occur during the second postnatal week (Ben-Ari et al., 2012), coinciding with the emergence of gamma band oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The composition of GABAA-receptor subunits changes during postnatal development, causing a progressive decrease of decay-time constants of inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) until they reach adult-like kinetics in the fourth postnatal week.
source: Moreover, the composition of GABAA-receptor subunits changes during postnatal development, causing a progressive decrease of decay-time constants of inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) until they reach adult-like kinetics in the fourth postnatal week (Okaty et al., 2009; Bosman et al., 2005; Laurie et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Simulations of neuronal networks proposed that increasing IPSCs kinetics in FS interneurons results in increasing gamma frequency.
source: Simulations of neuronal networks proposed that increasing IPSCs kinetics in FS interneurons results in increasing gamma frequency (Doischer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous modeling work.

claim: The gradual increase of prefrontal gamma frequency from the second to the fourth postnatal week provides experimental evidence for the hypothesis that increasing IPSCs kinetics results in increasing gamma frequency.
source: The gradual increase of prefrontal gamma frequency from the second to the fourth postnatal week provides experimental evidence for this hypothesis.
evidence: This claim connects the experimental findings to previous theoretical predictions.

claim: In patients and disease mouse models of schizophrenia and autism, gamma oscillations have been reported to be altered, likely to reflect abnormal pyramidal-interneuronal interactions.
source: Both, in patients and disease mouse models, gamma oscillations have been reported to be altered, likely to reflect abnormal pyramidal-interneuronal interactions (Cho et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2018; Rojas and Wilson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gamma dysfunction in neurodevelopmental disorders seems to emerge already during development.
source: These dysfunction seems to emerge already during development (Chini et al., 2020; Richter et al., 2019; Hartung et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Elucidating the developmental dynamics of cortical gamma activity might uncover the timeline of disease-related deficits.
source: Elucidating the developmental dynamics of cortical gamma activity might uncover the timeline of disease-related deficits.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential implications of the research.
